blocks.text: REST APIs and MCP servers are not competing answers to the same question, they answer two different questions that happen to look similar from a distance.
A REST API is how one piece of software asks another piece of software to do something, written for a developer who reads docs and writes code once.
MCP is about letting a language model figure out what it can do and call it itself, without a developer hardcoding that one specific call in advance.
1. The Problem REST APIs Solve
REST gives two separate systems, often built by different teams, a shared way to talk over HTTP using resources, verbs, and status codes.
It assumes a human developer is on the other end at design time, reading documentation and writing code that calls specific, known endpoints.
That code is written once, compiled or deployed, and then runs the same way every time it executes.
2. The Problem MCP Solves
MCP exists for a different situation, a language model that needs to decide at runtime what tools exist and how to use them.
No developer is sitting there wiring up each call ahead of time, the model itself has to read a description and choose.
MCP standardizes that discovery and calling convention so any model, talking to any compliant server, can do this the same way.
3. Same Underlying Transport, Different Job
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441592024-210214635.png
Under the hood, an MCP server is often just a small program that itself calls a REST API, a database, or some other backend.
MCP is not a replacement for REST inside the backend, it usually sits as a thin layer in front of it, aimed at a model instead of a human developer.
You can think of REST as the plumbing and MCP as the label on the pipe that tells a model what is flowing through it.

blocks.title: Keep this straight
blocks.content: MCP and REST usually work at different layers of the same system, not as two competing ways to build the same backend.

blocks.text: 4. Discoverability: Documentation Versus Self Description
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441592025-563670875.png
A REST API needs external documentation, a Swagger page, a wiki, a Postman collection, something a human reads before writing any calling code.
Nothing about hitting GET /users tells you that endpoint exists unless someone wrote that down somewhere first.
An MCP server is self describing, a client sends tools/list and gets back names, descriptions, and input schemas directly from the server itself.
There is no separate docs site to go stale, the description a model sees is generated live from the same code that runs the tool.
5. A REST Call That Requires Prior Knowledge
Here is a normal REST call, notice how much the developer already had to know before writing a single line.

code.content:
import requests

# a developer had to already know this exact path, method,
# and query parameter name from reading the docs beforehand
response = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/v2/orders",
    params={"status": "shipped"},
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + api_token}
)
orders = response.json()

blocks.text: If the endpoint moved to /v3/orders or renamed the status field, this code breaks and a human has to notice and fix it.
6. The Same Capability, Discovered Through MCP
Now compare that to how an MCP client finds the same capability, no prior knowledge of a URL is required at all.
The model reads that schema at runtime and decides how to fill it in, it never needed a docs page to know the tool existed.
7. How an LLM Actually Consumes a REST API

blocks.alt: How an LLM Actually Consumes a REST API
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441592025-31540117.png
An LLM cannot call a REST endpoint on its own, someone has to translate that endpoint into a tool schema the model is shown.
A developer writes that schema by hand, describing the endpoint, its parameters, and what it returns, in whatever format the model provider expects.
The model picks the tool by name and fills in arguments, then the developer's own code takes those arguments and makes the actual REST call.
8. How an LLM Actually Consumes an MCP Server
With MCP, the host application sends tools/list once at the start of a session and gets back live schemas straight from the server.
Those schemas get handed to the model exactly as returned, no developer had to transcribe or guess at them by hand.
When the model picks one, the host sends tools/call and the MCP server runs the real logic, often itself making a REST call behind the scenes.
9. Who Writes the Integration Code
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441592026-433469410.png
With plain REST, whoever builds the AI feature writes both the schema shown to the model and the code that executes the call.
With MCP, that work moves to whoever builds the MCP server, and every host that connects to it gets the integration for free.
That shift is the same reuse benefit teams get from any shared library, just applied specifically to how models discover and call tools.

blocks.text: 10. Statelessness Versus a Living Session
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441592026-345413356.png
REST is built to be stateless, each request carries everything needed and the server does not remember the last call.
MCP sessions are more like a conversation, a client connects, discovers what is available, and can keep calling tools across many turns.
This matters because an LLM is having an ongoing exchange, not firing one isolated request the way a simple REST client often does.
That said, individual tool calls inside an MCP session still look a lot like individual REST requests once you get past the discovery step.
11. Versioning and Change Over Time
A REST API that changes its shape usually needs a new version path, careful deprecation notices, and updated documentation everywhere.
An MCP server can add, remove, or change a tool and every connected model finds out the next time it asks, since the description is generated live.
This does not remove the need for careful change management, it just relocates discovery from static docs to a live call.
A breaking change to a tool schema can still confuse a model mid conversation, so thoughtful naming and clear descriptions still matter a great deal.
12. Security Still Works the Same Way Underneath
Wrapping a REST API in MCP does not remove the need for authentication, authorization, or rate limiting on the underlying service.
The MCP server still has to check who is calling it and what they are allowed to do, exactly like any REST backend would.
If anything, a model calling tools on its own makes those checks more important, since a person is no longer reviewing every single request by hand.

blocks.title: Common misconception
blocks.content: MCP is not a security layer by itself, it is a calling convention, the server behind it still needs real access controls.

blocks.text: 13. When You Would Still Reach for Plain REST

blocks.alt: When You Would Still Reach for Plain REST
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441592026-553906647.png
Not every feature needs an LLM in the loop, and plain REST is often still the right and simpler choice.

items: A normal web or mobile app calling your own backend, with no model deciding anything.
Service to service calls between two systems your own team fully controls end to end.
A single, tightly scoped internal script that will never be exposed to a model at all.
High throughput, low latency paths where the extra hop through a discovery step adds cost you cannot afford.
A one-off integration you are confident nobody else, human or model, will ever need to reuse.

blocks.text: 14. When Wrapping That Same API in MCP Pays Off

blocks.alt: When Wrapping That Same API in MCP Pays Off
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441592027-75754616.png
The calculus flips once more than one AI agent or model provider might need the same capability.
A single MCP server in front of an existing REST API lets any compliant model discover and call it, without a developer writing a new schema for every new assistant.
It also pays off once the underlying API keeps changing, since new tools show up automatically instead of waiting on a manual schema update.
Worked Example
Picture a company with an existing orders REST API, already used by its web app and mobile app for years.
Now the company wants a chat assistant that can answer "where is my order" questions by calling that same backend.
Option one, hardcode a tool schema in the chat app that calls the REST endpoint directly, quick to build for exactly one assistant.
Option two, wrap that same REST call inside a small MCP server, then any assistant the company builds next can reuse it with zero new schema work.
If only one chat assistant will ever need this, option one is fine, if a Slack bot and a support tool will also need it soon, option two saves real time.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming MCP replaces REST, most MCP servers still call a REST API or database underneath, they do not compete with it.
Wrapping a tiny, single use internal endpoint in MCP out of habit, when no model will ever call it more than once.
Forgetting that an MCP server still needs its own authentication and permission checks, MCP is not a security feature by itself.
Treating tools/list as a one time setup step instead of something a host should call again when it expects new tools to appear.
Writing a REST style hardcoded tool schema by hand for an LLM feature when an existing MCP server already covers that same capability.

blocks.text: Practice
Pick one REST endpoint you already know well, maybe one from your own project or a public API you have used.

code.content:
endpoint = "GET /v2/orders/{id}"
used_by_more_than_one_ai_client_soon = True  # or False
needs_a_model_to_decide_when_to_call_it = True  # or False
# if both are True, sketch it as an MCP tool instead of a hardcoded schema

blocks.text: Write down its schema the way you would hand it to a model directly, then write it again as an MCP tool definition, and compare how each would age as the API changes.
Key Takeaway
REST solves communication between two systems that already know about each other ahead of time, MCP solves discovery and calling for a model that does not.
Most of the time an MCP server is a thin, self describing layer sitting in front of a perfectly normal REST API underneath, not a replacement for it.
